subject: chemistry

moments.title: Natural isotopes and transmutation
moments.body:
Rutherford in 1919 demonstrates the first artificial transmutation: alpha + nitrogen → oxygen-17 + proton. Aston perfects the mass spectrograph (1919) and shows elements are mixtures of isotopes. Chadwick discovers the neutron (1932).

By 1933 the elementary nuclear physics is in place, but all known radioactive elements are still naturally occurring. The Joliot-Curies will change that.
moments.takeaway: Nuclear bombardment can change elements. But all known radioactive isotopes remain natural.

moments.title: Joliot-Curies miss the neutron and the positron
moments.body:
Working at the Radium Institute, the Joliot-Curies observe a 'mysterious radiation' from beryllium when bombarded with alpha particles. They publish — but interpret it as gamma rays. Chadwick reads their paper, immediately realises it's a neutral particle of nucleon mass, and discovers the neutron.

They also observe positrons emitted from beryllium and aluminium under alpha bombardment — but again interpret them as protons. Anderson (Caltech, 1932) wins the credit for the positron.

Twice missed in 18 months.
moments.takeaway: Even great experimentalists can misinterpret their own data. The Joliot-Curies are determined not to miss the next one.

moments.title: Artificial radioactivity discovered
moments.body:
On 11 January 1934, the Joliot-Curies bombard aluminium foil with alpha particles from a polonium source. They notice that after removing the polonium source, the aluminium continues to emit radiation — for several minutes — before going quiet.

They have created phosphorus-30, a radioactive isotope that does not occur in nature. Its half-life is 2.5 minutes; it decays by positron emission to silicon-30.

Alpha + aluminium-27 → phosphorus-30 + neutron.
moments.takeaway: Radioactivity can be made on demand. Any element could potentially be made radioactive by nuclear bombardment.

moments.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry
moments.body:
The Joliot-Curies share the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. They are the second married couple to share a Nobel — the first being Marie and Pierre Curie in 1903. Irène is the daughter of those laureates.

Marie Curie had died of aplastic anaemia in July 1934, six months after her daughter's discovery and one year before the Nobel announcement.
moments.takeaway: A second-generation Nobel. The Curie/Joliot-Curie family becomes the most-laureated in scientific history.

now.title: Artificial isotopes today
now.body:
About 3000 isotopes are known across 118 elements; most are made artificially. Medical isotopes (Tc-99m for SPECT imaging, F-18 for PET, I-131 for thyroid therapy) are routinely made in reactors and cyclotrons.

Fermi extended the Joliot-Curies' work using neutrons instead of alphas (Rome, 1934 onwards) and produced many new isotopes — and (unknowingly) the first products of uranium fission, recognised as such by Hahn, Strassmann and Meitner in 1938.
now.open_questions: How far can the chart of nuclides extend? Where are the limits of nuclear stability (the 'drip lines')? Can we synthesise long-lived superheavy elements at the predicted 'island of stability'?

reflection: Both Joliot-Curies died of radiation-related illness — Irène of leukaemia in 1956, Frédéric of liver disease in 1958. Two generations of Curie women died of their work. How do we evaluate the moral economy of scientific discovery when the discoverers themselves are killed by what they uncover?
